rows.stem: Explain, giving two reasons, how immune response by "vaccine" is different from that by "antitoxin" in humans.
rows.solution:
A vaccine and an antitoxin both protect the body, but they do it in different ways. Any two of these differences:

| Immune response by vaccine | Immune response by antitoxin |
|---|---|
| The body **makes its own antibodies** in response to the weakened or killed antigen introduced in the vaccine. | **Preformed antibodies** (the antitoxin) are injected directly into the body. |
| The response **takes some time** to develop. | The response is **quick**, as the antibodies are ready-made. |
| **Memory B and T cells are generated**, so the protection is long lasting. | It is a **one-time response**: no memory cells are formed and the protection is short-lived. |
| It gives **active immunity**. | It gives **passive immunity**. |

For example, in a snakebite or tetanus the antitoxin is injected because the patient needs antibodies immediately and cannot wait for the body to make them.

rows.stem: Mention the common bacterium found in the anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment and also in the rumen of cattle. How is this bacterium commercially useful ?
rows.solution:
The bacterium is **Methanobacterium**, a **methanogen**. It grows anaerobically in the anaerobic sludge digesters of sewage treatment plants and also in the rumen (part of the stomach) of cattle, where it breaks down cellulose.

It is commercially useful because it **produces biogas (gobar gas)**. Methanogens growing anaerobically on cellulosic material produce large amounts of **methane** along with carbon dioxide and hydrogen. This gas is used as a fuel for cooking and lighting, and cattle dung, which is rich in these bacteria, is the feed of biogas plants.

rows.stem: Name the effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens belonging to group of viruses. Also write about the ways they support the environment.
Some of the microbes used as biofertilizers are prokaryotes. Name the taxonomic group they come under. With the help of an example, mention how they act as biofertilizers.
rows.solution:
These prokaryotic biofertilisers are **bacteria**, including the **cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)**, all placed in the kingdom Monera.

Example: **Rhizobium**, which lives symbiotically in the **root nodules of leguminous plants**. It **fixes atmospheric nitrogen into organic forms** that the plant uses as nutrient, so it enriches the nitrogen content of the soil and increases its fertility.

Other examples that act the same way: the free-living bacteria Azospirillum and Azotobacter, and the cyanobacteria Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria, which fix nitrogen in paddy fields.

rows.stem: Different species belonging to genus Trichoderma are useful to humans as well as to plants. Justify their roles by giving one instance of each.
rows.solution:
- **Useful to plants:** species of Trichoderma are free-living fungi common in root ecosystems, and they are **effective biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens**, so crops can be protected without chemical fungicides.
- **Useful to humans:** Trichoderma polysporum produces **cyclosporin A**, which is used as an **immunosuppressive agent** in organ-transplant patients, so that the body does not reject the transplanted organ.

rows.stem:
The figures given below show the results of a lab experiment in which two microbial species A and B belonging to same genus were grown in three petri dishes having same culture medium. In Petri dish-I, Species-A was grown alone for 8 weeks. In Petri dish-II, Species-B was grown alone for 8 weeks. In Petri dish-III, both the species were grown together with the same number as Petri dish-I and Petri dish-II for 8 weeks.
What conclusion will you draw from the graphs in terms of impact of interaction on growth ? Explain, giving reason.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:three side-by-side graphs of No. of individuals (y, 0 to 200) against Time (in weeks) (x, 0 to 8), titled Petri dish-I 'Sp. A grown alone', Petri dish-II 'Sp. B grown alone' and Petri dish-III 'Sp. A and B grown together'; Sp. A is drawn as a dashed curve and Sp. B as a solid curve, each rising from near 20 and levelling off. The level at which each species levels off alone versus together decides the conclusion the question asks for, so those heights are withheld here. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
**Both species show better growth when they are grown together.** In Petri dish-III each species levels off at a higher number than it reaches when grown alone: Species A at about 175 individuals instead of about 145, and Species B at about 115 instead of about 85.

Reason: since each population grows better in the presence of the other, **both species benefit from the interaction**. An interaction in which both interacting species benefit is **mutualism**, so species A and B show mutualism.

rows.stem:
The graphs given below, A and B, represent population of elephants in two different National Parks (a hypothetical situation) at different times.
Study the graphs and comment upon the pattern of growth observed. Mention the possible reason for such patterns seen in nature.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:two graphs of Elephant population (y) against Year (x): graph A with the y axis marked 0, 2000, 4000, 6000, 7000 and the x axis 1900 to 1980; graph B with the y axis marked 0 to 2000 in steps of 500 and the x axis 1960 to 2010. The shape of each curve is exactly the growth pattern the question asks the student to name, so it is withheld here. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
- **Graph A** shows **exponential (geometric) growth**: the elephant population rises slowly at first and then faster and faster, from almost zero in 1900 to over 7000 by the 1950s, giving a J-shaped curve. This happens when **resources are unlimited** and there are **no checks or environmental resistance** on the population, so it grows at its full intrinsic rate.
- **Graph B** shows a **steep decline towards extinction**: the population falls from over 2000 around 1970 to almost zero by 2000. This happens when **resources are lacking** and the **environmental resistance** (shortage of food and space, and threats such as poaching and habitat loss) is high, so deaths far exceed births.

rows.stem: As per a recent newspaper report, a particular country showed declining population growth rate. According to you, what could be the two most possible reasons for this decline and why ?
rows.solution:
The size of a population changes as:

\(N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]\)

where \(B\) is births (natality), \(I\) immigration, \(D\) deaths (mortality) and \(E\) emigration. The growth rate falls whenever additions fall or losses rise. Two likely reasons for the country (any two):
- **Decreased birth rate (natality)**, for example through the **use of contraceptives** and family planning, so fewer individuals are added.
- **Increased mortality**, for example from the **spread of an epidemic**, so more individuals are lost.
- **Increased emigration**, as people leave the country, for example in search of jobs.

The marking scheme also accepts the question read for plants and animals, where deforestation, decreased food availability, predation pressure, adverse weather or competition are the reasons.

rows.subtopic: Species Numbers and Patterns of Biodiversity
rows.stem:
The graph given below shows species-area relationship of a certain region.
(i) Study the graph and explain what it represents.
(ii) After a while, a small area was taken for constructing a road which divided the region into two. Write the impact this construction would have on species richness of the region.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a single curve of No. of species (y, 0 to 500 in steps of 100) against Area evaluated (in hectares) (x, 0 to 60 in steps of 10), starting at the origin. The shape of the curve is what part (i) asks the student to explain, so it is withheld here. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
(i) The graph shows the **species-area relationship** described by Alexander von Humboldt: **within a region, species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit**. The number of species rises steeply over the first 10 to 20 hectares and then levels off at about 440 species. On a normal scale this relationship is a rectangular hyperbola, and on a log scale it is a straight line:

\(\log S = \log C + Z \log A\)

where \(S\) is species richness, \(A\) is area, \(Z\) is the slope of the line (regression coefficient) and \(C\) is the Y-intercept.

(ii) The road **fragments the habitat** into two smaller pieces. Each piece has a smaller area, so by the species-area relationship it can hold fewer species, and animals that need large territories (and some migratory animals) are badly affected. So the construction will have a **negative impact on species richness**: the species diversity of the region will be **gradually reduced**, with the impact becoming visible only slowly.

rows.stem: How did Dr. David Tilman relate experimentally, the stability of a community and its species richness ? Explain.
rows.solution:
David Tilman carried out **long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots**:
- He found that **plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass**, that is, they were more stable.
- He also showed that in his experiments **increased diversity (species richness) contributed to higher productivity**.

So a community with more species is more stable: it resists occasional disturbance and its productivity does not vary much from year to year.

rows.stem: What are the consequences of loss of biodiversity in a region ? Explain.
Bacillus thuringiensis plays an important role in Integrated Pest Management strategy. Explain how. Name any two crops that are protected efficiently from pests.
rows.solution:
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is a microbial biocontrol agent, so it lets farmers control insect pests with little or no chemical pesticide, which is the aim of integrated pest management:
- **Dried spores of Bt** are available in sachets. They are **mixed with water and sprayed onto vulnerable plants**.
- The spores are **eaten by the insect larvae**; in the gut the **toxin is released and the larvae are killed**. The bacterial disease kills the caterpillars but leaves other insects unharmed.
- Two crops protected this way: **Brassicas** and **fruit trees**.

Scientists have also **introduced the Bt toxin genes into plants**, which then make the toxin themselves, so the insect dies when it eats the plant. The marking scheme accepts this route too, with crops such as **Bt cotton**, Bt corn, Bt rice, Bt tomato, Bt potato and Bt soybean.

rows.stem: With the help of a storyboard or a flowchart only, explain all the stages of how human insulin is produced through r-DNA technology.
rows.solution:
Human insulin is made of two short polypeptide chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges. In 1983, Eli Lilly produced it by r-DNA technology in these stages:

Two DNA sequences corresponding to the **A and B chains** of human insulin are prepared
\(\downarrow\)
Each is **introduced into plasmids of E. coli**
\(\downarrow\)
The bacteria produce the **chains A and B separately**
\(\downarrow\)
Chains A and B are **extracted**
\(\downarrow\)
The two chains are **combined by creating disulphide bonds** to form **human insulin**

The marking scheme gives the same marks when the stages are shown as a storyboard instead of a flowchart.

rows.stem:
(a) Explain the roles of (i) primary, and (ii) secondary lymphoid organs that are responsible for developing defence to combat the action of pathogens/foreign antigens which enter our body.
(b) Doctors generally advise not to undergo surgery of tonsils. Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) (i) **Primary lymphoid organs** (the **bone marrow** and the **thymus**) are where lymphocytes originate and mature: here the **immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes**. The bone marrow produces all blood cells including lymphocytes, and the thymus provides the micro-environment for the development and maturation of **T-lymphocytes**.

(ii) **Secondary lymphoid organs** (the **spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine, appendix** and the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) receive the mature lymphocytes. They **trap the microorganisms or antigens** and **provide the sites for the interaction of lymphocytes with the antigen**, after which the lymphocytes proliferate to become **effector cells** that give the immune response.

(b) The **tonsils are secondary lymphoid organs**. They trap the antigens (pathogens) that enter through the mouth and nose, and provide a site where lymphocytes interact with these antigens and are activated to become effector cells. Removing them takes away this early defence, so doctors generally advise against the surgery.

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem:
Causative agents of HIV-AIDS and COVID-19 belong to the same group of viruses. To diagnose and amplify the genetic material for further study of COVID-19 virus, 'RT-PCR' test is carried out.
(a) What does 'RT-PCR' stand for ?
(b) Explain the various steps of PCR technique.
rows.solution:
CBSE awarded the 1 mark for part (a) to every student who attempted it.

(a) RT-PCR stands for **Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction** (RT for reverse transcriptase). Both HIV and the COVID-19 virus have **RNA** as their genetic material, so the RNA is first copied into DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase, and this DNA is then amplified by PCR. (The marking scheme also accepts "Real Time Polymerase Chain Reaction"; the COVID-19 test is in fact a real-time RT-PCR, in which the amplification is followed as it happens.)

(b) PCR makes multiple copies of a gene (or DNA) in vitro, using two sets of primers and the enzyme DNA polymerase. Each cycle has three steps:
- **Denaturation:** the double-stranded DNA is **heated**, so its two strands separate.
- **Annealing:** two **primers** (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides) join to the **complementary regions** of the DNA, one on each strand.
- **Extension:** the primers are extended by a **thermostable DNA polymerase**, **Taq polymerase** (isolated from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus), using the deoxynucleotides provided; the enzyme stays active through the high temperature of denaturation.

The cycle is **repeated many times**, and the DNA segment is amplified up to approximately a billion copies.

rows.stem: Write your interpretation, with reason, on the basis of the three parameters plotted in the graph.
rows.context: There are two different farm lands, one where Bt-cotton crop was cultivated and the other where non Bt-cotton crop (indigenous) was cultivated. Farmers responsible for this experimental cultivation were free to use the farming practices of their choice. During the cultivation period, the data was collected with respect to the amount of pesticide used, water required for irrigation and at harvesting time, the crop productivity. Based on the data collected, a bar graph was plotted which is shown below.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:a bar graph of Number/Litres (y, 0 to 120 in steps of 20) for three groups along an x axis titled Inputs: Crop productivity (Tonnes/Ha), Pesticide (Litres/Ha) and Irrigation (Litres/Ha), with two bars per group keyed Non-Bt average (a crazed, cobblestone pattern) and Bt average (a square grid). The bar heights, and so which crop is higher on each parameter, are what the question asks the student to interpret, so they are withheld here. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Reading the three pairs of bars:
- **Crop productivity:** about 120 for Bt cotton against about 80 for non-Bt cotton, so **productivity is much higher in the Bt crop**, because the Bt crop is protected from its insect pests.
- **Pesticide:** about 80 for Bt cotton against about 100 for non-Bt cotton, so **pesticide use is reduced in the Bt crop**, as it makes its own insecticidal protein. This saves resources and is environment friendly.
- **Irrigation:** about 60 for Bt cotton against about 40 for non-Bt cotton, so the **Bt crop requires more water** than the non-Bt crop.

rows.stem: Which one of the crops would you like to cultivate in your farm and why ?
rows.context: There are two different farm lands, one where Bt-cotton crop was cultivated and the other where non Bt-cotton crop (indigenous) was cultivated. Farmers responsible for this experimental cultivation were free to use the farming practices of their choice. During the cultivation period, the data was collected with respect to the amount of pesticide used, water required for irrigation and at harvesting time, the crop productivity. Based on the data collected, a bar graph was plotted which is shown below.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's bar graph (Non-Bt average and Bt average bars for Crop productivity, Pesticide and Irrigation, y axis Number/Litres 0 to 120); weighing the bars decides which crop to choose, so their heights are withheld here. Page idx 10.
rows.solution: I would cultivate **Bt cotton**. Weighing all three parameters, the Bt crop is more beneficial to the farmer: it gives **more output** while needing **less pesticide**, and that gain outweighs its higher need for water where irrigation is available.

rows.stem: Which one out of these two crops would a farmer from Rajasthan like to cultivate and why ?
rows.context: There are two different farm lands, one where Bt-cotton crop was cultivated and the other where non Bt-cotton crop (indigenous) was cultivated. Farmers responsible for this experimental cultivation were free to use the farming practices of their choice. During the cultivation period, the data was collected with respect to the amount of pesticide used, water required for irrigation and at harvesting time, the crop productivity. Based on the data collected, a bar graph was plotted which is shown below.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the case study's bar graph (Non-Bt average and Bt average bars for Crop productivity, Pesticide and Irrigation, y axis Number/Litres 0 to 120); which crop needs more irrigation water decides the answer, so the heights are withheld here. Page idx 10.
rows.solution: A farmer from Rajasthan would prefer the **non-Bt cotton crop**. Rajasthan is a dry region where there is usually a **shortage of water**, and the graph shows that the non-Bt crop needs **less water for irrigation** than the Bt crop.

rows.stem:
(i) What do 'EcoR I', 'BamH I' and 'Hind III' represent ? State their functions.
(ii) Identify the gene you would select for the role of a selectable marker in pBR322. Explain why.
(iii) Write the property/characteristic of plasmid and bacteriophage that makes them efficient cloning vectors.
(iv) Biotechnologists always insert 'ori' gene in their engineered cloning vector. Justify the statement.
(v) Will the experiment be successful if the alien DNA is ligated at Hind III restriction site ? Give reason in support of your answer.
rows.context: Gene of interest/alien gene is introduced by a cloning vector into a host cell to bring about a desired phenotypic expression in a host cell. The cloning vectors used are plasmid and bacteriophages. Biotechnologists in their labs, for desired results engineered specialised cloning vectors. One such vector is pBR322. Study the diagram carefully and answer the questions that follow.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED:the NCERT map of the plasmid pBR322: a double ring labelled pBR322 with the regions ampR, tetR, ori and rop marked inside it, and restriction sites labelled round the outside: EcoR I, Cla I and Hind III at the top, Pvu I and Pst I at the upper left, BamH I at the upper right, Sal I at the right and Pvu II at the bottom. Which gene region each site falls in, and in particular where Hind III sits relative to ampR and tetR, decides parts (ii) and (v), so the site-to-gene placement is withheld here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(i) EcoR I, BamH I and Hind III are **restriction endonucleases** (restriction enzymes); in the map they mark their **recognition (restriction) sites** in pBR322. They act as **molecular scissors**: each recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence and **cuts the DNA at a specific site** within it, leaving sticky ends to which foreign DNA cut by the same enzyme can be joined.

(ii) I would select an antibiotic resistance gene, **ampR** (ampicillin resistance) or **tetR** (tetracycline resistance). A selectable marker **helps in identifying and selecting transformants from non-transformants**: only cells that have taken up the plasmid grow on a medium containing the antibiotic. When foreign DNA is inserted inside one of these genes, that resistance is lost (insertional inactivation), so **recombinants can also be identified from non-recombinants**.

(iii) Plasmids and bacteriophages can **replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of the chromosomal DNA** (autonomous replication). Bacteriophages, because of their high number per cell, and some plasmids have a **very high copy number**, so they replicate the desired gene into a large number of copies. (The marking scheme also accepts the presence of a selectable marker, of cloning sites, or of ori.)

(iv) **ori** is the **sequence from where replication starts**. Any piece of DNA linked to it can be made to replicate within the host cell, and ori is also responsible for **controlling the copy number** of the linked DNA. Without ori the vector, and the alien gene in it, would not be multiplied, which is why it is always included.

(v) **No.** In the map the Hind III site lies outside both the ampR and the tetR genes, so alien DNA ligated there inactivates neither antibiotic resistance gene. Bacteria carrying the recombinant plasmid would then grow on both ampicillin and tetracycline, exactly like those carrying the plain plasmid, so **recombinants could not be identified from non-recombinants**. Transformants as such could still be picked out on an antibiotic, since both resistance genes stay intact; it is the recombinants that cannot be told apart.
